strengths: Comprehensive evaluation on 9 medical imaging datasets with multiple types of distribution shifts (modalities, pathologies, institutions)
Strong and consistent empirical results with substantial improvements under large distribution shifts (e.g., 11.9% over TSCA on T1 modality) while maintaining performance under small shifts
Practical efficiency advantage: achieves best results with only 2 backpropagations per image compared to 10+ for competing methods
Well-designed two-stage approach with intuitive motivation: Stage 1 for segmentation ability, Stage 2 for click leveraging
Thorough ablation study (Fig. 3) demonstrating necessity of both stages and GPL contribution to online adaptation performance
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of the method pipeline and results across diverse datasets
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: GPL is a straightforward Gaussian-weighted masked cross-entropy loss; two-stage adaptation is intuitive but simple; using pseudo ground truth is standard practice
Critical reliance on pseudo ground truth quality without analysis of robustness to corrupted labels or base model underperformance under large distribution shifts

Simulated clicks rather than real user interactions: automatically generated with deterministic placement strategy, no evaluation of robustness to actual clinician click patterns or different interaction strategies
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; results averaged over only 3 runs without reporting variance or statistical tests
Narrow baseline comparisons limited to IA+SA and TSCA; missing comparisons with broader test-time adaptation literature and other recent interactive segmentation methods
Hyperparameter justification lacking: α=0.7, β=200, σ=3 introduced without ablation or sensitivity analysis; unclear selection methodology risks overfitting to test sets
Potential catastrophic forgetting not addressed: continuous adaptation could degrade performance on original training distribution, but no evaluation of this concern
Lack of failure analysis and qualitative evaluation: no discussion of failure modes, limited visualization of segmentation improvements, no per-dataset analysis of improvement sources
Ad-hoc Stage 2 click generation strategy: one click per error region lacks principled justification and no comparison with alternative point generation strategies
Missing computational analysis: no reporting of per-image adaptation time, memory requirements, or total deployment cost despite efficiency claims

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 medical imaging datasets (5 fundus, 4 brain MRI) with multiple types of distribution shifts (modalities, pathologies), demonstrating broad applicability
Addresses a practical and clinically relevant problem of adapting segmentation models to post-deployment data distributions using natural user feedback
Consistent empirical improvements over baselines (IA+SA, TSCA), with particularly strong results on challenging scenarios (e.g., ATLAS: 81.8% vs 64.0%)
Computational efficiency: requires only 2 backpropagation steps per image compared to 10 for TSCA
Ablation studies (Fig. 3) demonstrate the importance of both stages and components
Clear presentation with informative figures, particularly Fig. 1 showing the overall method pipeline
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Gaussian Point Loss is straightforward Gaussian-weighted cross-entropy (arbitrary design choices: σ=3, 10-pixel radius with no ablation); two-stage approach is standard fine-tuning; combines existing techniques without significant methodological innovation

Problematic core assumption: using final prediction after T=10 corrections as pseudo-ground truth is never validated—no analysis of pseudo-label quality, and when base model performs poorly (e.g., 20% Dice), 10 clicks may be insufficient to create correct targets

Simulated user interactions lack clinical validation: automatic point generation in error regions likely differs from real clinician behavior; no user studies demonstrating that simulated clicks represent actual clinical patterns; critical limitation for a paper claiming practical applicability

Limited and potentially unfair baseline comparisons: only 2 online adaptation baselines; missing modern test-time adaptation methods and simple baselines to isolate GPL contribution; TSCA vs OAIMS comparison uses different update regimes (10 vs 2 steps)—unclear if improvements come from the method or regularization effect

Unclear component contributions: ablation doesn't cleanly isolate GPL's contribution from the two-stage strategy; it's unclear whether improvements derive from novelty or from simply using fewer training iterations

Insufficient experimental rigor: only 3 runs with no confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance testing; small datasets (<150 cases) with different hyperparameters per dataset suggest potential overfitting; different learning rates (10⁻⁴ vs 5×10⁻⁵) not justified

Missing critical analyses: no failure mode discussion, no study of distribution shift magnitude effects, no visualization of model evolution over image sequences, single online sequence shown in Fig. 3 bottom without multiple trials

Technical clarity issues: GPL normalization by |u|·H·W produces very small values; indicator function I seems unnecessarily complex; unclear if model is reset between sequences or if catastrophic forgetting occurs; update schedule (per image vs multiple epochs) undefined

Limited evaluation: only Dice score reported; missing HD95, sensitivity, specificity, and error-type analysis (FP vs FN); 2D brain MRI experiments use only single largest lesion slice, limiting clinical relevance; method only tested on U-Net architecture
Pseudo-ground truth validation absent: no comparison of pseudo-label quality against manual annotations; no analysis of how pseudo-label errors propagate through Stage 2 optimization

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 medical imaging databases with multiple distribution shift types (modalities, pathologies), demonstrating consistent improvements over baselines
Practical and efficient approach requiring only 2 backpropagations per image vs. 10+ for competitors, suitable for clinical deployment
Well-motivated problem addressing post-deployment model adaptation using user corrections, which is clinically relevant
Solid empirical results with substantial improvements on large distribution shifts (e.g., 11.9% gain over TSCA on BRATS T1 modality shift)
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and ablation study demonstrating contribution of all components
Simple, principled two-stage approach that separately optimizes segmentation ability and click utilization
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: GPL is straightforward Gaussian-weighted cross-entropy loss, two-stage adaptation is intuitive but conceptually simple, pseudo ground truth supervision is standard practice
GPL design lacks theoretical justification: 10-pixel radius threshold and σ=3 parameter appear arbitrary with no ablation studies or comparison to alternative spatial weighting schemes

Methodological circularity concern: Stage 2 click generation relies on comparing model output with pseudo ground truth, introducing circular dependency and making the claim of 'no clinician help needed' misleading

Incomplete baseline comparisons: only compares with older methods (IA+SA, TSCA); MedSAM adapter comparison is superficial; no comparison with recent interactive segmentation or online adaptation methods

Evaluation limitations: uses simulated automated click generation instead of real user behavior; no user study validation; 2D-only evaluation despite 3D database availability; marginal improvements on some datasets lack error bars or confidence intervals
Limited scope: restricted to medical imaging, relatively simple segmentation tasks, only tested on ISFCNN base model; no analysis of failure cases or pseudo ground truth quality
Missing ablations on key design choices: no sensitivity analysis on β=200, α=0.7 hyperparameters; different learning rates for fundus vs. MRI unexplained; no ablation on Gaussian radius
Reproducibility concerns: missing implementation details on Stage 2 initialization, no computational cost/runtime analysis, promise of code only upon publication

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 medical imaging datasets with diverse distribution shifts, including thorough ablation studies and robustness testing (extreme domain shifts, noisy inputs, poor pseudo-labels)
Strong and consistent empirical results with 10%+ Dice improvements on brain MRI over SOTA methods (TSCA, IA+SA) and achievement of target performance with significantly fewer clicks
Practical and computationally efficient method with low latency (0.05-0.41s), clear presentation, and detailed algorithmic descriptions supporting reproducibility
Well-motivated problem addressing genuine distribution shift challenges in medical imaging deployment through an intuitive interactive segmentation paradigm
Solid technical execution with thorough ablations clearly demonstrating the contribution of each component (CCG loss, Post-Interaction, Mid-Interaction adaptation)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: CCG loss is a straightforward Gaussian-weighted cross-entropy extension; pseudo-label learning from user corrections is intuitive but conceptually standard; the contribution is primarily an effective combination of existing techniques rather than novel concepts

Unfair baseline comparisons: Reimplemented baselines (IA+SA, TSCA) use the authors' CCG loss pretraining, conflating improvements from novel adaptation strategy vs. better pretraining; unclear whether superior performance stems from online adaptation innovation or pretraining changes

Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests for main results; only 3 random seeds reported for one ablation without standard deviations; difficult to assess if improvements are statistically significant

Pseudo ground-truth assumption vulnerability: Central assumption that user-corrected masks are 'good enough' quality can fail critically; in extreme shifts (BRATS→ATLAS), base model achieves only 9.3% Dice with 1 click; early poor pseudo-labels could cause error accumulation

Reliance on simulated user interactions: All experiments use automatic click placement in erroneous regions; real clinicians may place clicks differently; systematic bias in click placement could favor the method, limiting confidence in clinical translation

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 medical imaging databases with diverse distribution shifts (modalities, pathologies, scanners)
Strong and consistent empirical results, especially on brain MRI (>10% Dice improvements over TSCA)
Extensive ablation studies and robustness testing including wrong clicks, extreme domain gaps, and multi-database scenarios
Practical considerations addressed (latency analysis: 0.05s GPU/0.25s CPU)
Thorough evaluation of edge cases and failure modes (pseudo-label quality, overfitting with 50 clicks, shuffled databases)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: method primarily combines existing online learning techniques with a simple Gaussian-weighted CE loss; pseudo-label usage in semi-supervised learning is well-established
Critical validation gap: all experiments use simulated automatic clicks; no user study to validate that real clinicians would follow predicted patterns or find the interactive workflow practical

Pseudo ground-truth assumption is strong but under-justified: no principled criteria for determining when P_final is 'good enough' to serve as pseudo-label; potential for error accumulation especially in early iterations
No statistical rigor: main results tables (1-4) lack error bars or confidence intervals; improvements sometimes modest (1-2% Dice) with unclear significance
Hyperparameter selection concerns: claims no tuning but uses α=0.7, β=200, σ=3 from unspecified 'preliminary experiments'; Table 12 shows high sensitivity to β and σ
Baseline fairness issues: Med-SA frozen during testing (unfair to SAM); re-implemented baselines by authors raise implementation bias concerns; no evaluation of fine-tuned SAM
Limited architectural scope: only U-Net despite claiming model-agnostic; no evaluation on Transformers or other modern architectures; click encoding strategy is architecture-specific
Key algorithms (1-2) relegated to appendix; dense Figure 1 hard to parse; implementation details missing (optimizer, learning rates for adaptation, gradient steps per update)
Reproducibility concerns: code unavailable for review (promised 'upon publication'), TBI dataset non-public, re-implemented baselines without official implementations
Incomplete analysis: Stage 2 click generation quality not analyzed; no comparison to simpler test-time adaptation; limited investigation into why Med-SA underperforms

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing real distribution shifts in medical imaging deployment
Comprehensive experimental validation across 9 diverse medical imaging databases with multiple types of distribution shifts
Strong empirical results with substantial improvements on challenging scenarios (10%+ Dice on BRATS T1)
Extensive and thorough ablation studies (Tables 5-7) and robustness analysis (Tables 8-11) demonstrating resilience to extreme domain shifts, wrong clicks, and mixed domains
Simple but effective approach avoiding complex regularization mechanisms of prior work
Practical design with negligible computational cost (0.25-0.41s on CPU) and model-agnostic applicability
Clear presentation, reproducibility, and algorithmic descriptions (Algorithms 1-2) with promised code release
Effective robustness to realistic failure modes including 40% wrong user clicks and extreme domain gaps
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—individual components (pseudo-labeling, Gaussian weighting) are well-known; CCG loss is essentially weighted cross-entropy with class masking
Evaluation relies exclusively on simulated user clicks via deterministic largest-error strategy rather than real clinician interactions
CCG loss design choice (Eq. 2 indicator function) limits learning signal when model predicts wrong class in clicked regions; mechanism deserves deeper analysis despite ablation support
Pseudo-ground-truth quality not formally defined with explicit thresholds—assumes any user correction is suitable for learning
Moderate improvements in some settings (fundus databases: 1-2% gains vs brain MRI: 10%+); disc segmentation near-perfect across methods
Limited comparison scope—only two online adaptation baselines (IA+SA, TSCA); missing comparisons with other test-time/domain adaptation methods from broader literature
Hyperparameter sensitivity not fully addressed—σ=0 extremely unstable (46.9-83.2% variance); β and σ require careful tuning
Incomplete complementarity of Post- and Mid-Interaction mechanisms (Table 6: PI benefits diminish beyond ~5 clicks)
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals; results appear to be single runs
Generalization limited to point clicks; no evaluation on scribbles or bounding boxes
Potential source domain performance degradation (2.9% Dice drop) requires re-adaptation mitigation overhead
Missing real clinician user studies and 3D volume evaluation; evaluation restricted to 2D slices and binary/few-class tasks
